Matched passages: §135 · §140 · §166 · §168 · §193 · §204 · §205 · §231

Download original message (.eml)

As an "average person" who, against type (according to Mr. Ric Gonzales), 
does NOT "seek
distractions, illusions and stupid comforts over cruel and abrupt 
honesty", I have decided to
neglect my usual pastime of self-flagellation and enter the fray of mass 
flagellation presented
herein regarding TK's life and alleged works with a few stray comments.

A few caveats:   I am an (unpublished) writer and former student of 
psychology.  I have no
logical, mathematical or analytical skills, and can't argue my way out of 
a paper bag, but I have
been told that I can write a complete sentence, so perhaps my stay in your 
midst will be longer
than Mr. Meredith's.

Mr. Ric Gonzales opines:

>You [Mignarda?] and others have to realize that the genius mind is 
>extremely active
>and seeking complexity.  You won't find too many geniuses who take much 
>of an interest in the
>trivialities that most people endure (or prefer).

I must have missed the beginning, but just exactly what defines "the 
genius mind"?  Is it a
certain level of IQ?  Is it a certain level of antisocialization?  Is it a 
certain elevated level of
intellectual snobbery?  I would suggest that a good majority of the 
members of this group have
above average levels of intelligence, antisocialization, and cerebral 
superiority (I include myself
in the last two).  I would also suggest that the august Ms. Asia, for 
example, long may she reign,
possesses both a ferocious intelligence (and perhaps even a MENSA 
membership) and an
almost Rabelaisian appetite for every triviality known to peoplekind.  A 
concrete definition would
ease my diminutive mind.

Now  to the argument over the Manifesto, which Mr. Mignarda calls 
"doggerel", a term,
unfortunately, pertaining only to _verse_

	trivial, poorly constructed verse, usually of a burlesque or comic 
sort; jingle

			-Webster's New World Dictionary

which description is certainly antithetical to the Manifesto, but no 
matter, unless Mr. Mignarda
thinks it's a prose poem...

I can't offer an opinion whether it's a

>total ripoff of Ellul's ideas

because I was too busy chasing geologists and getting drunk in college to 
peruse that
gentleman's works, and if Mr. Mignarda would be so kind as to provide a 
quick summary I could
foster an opinion.

It appears to be Mr. Mignarda's thesis that

>[TK wishes to] liberate us from the enervating effects of technology by 
>enslaving us to his
>will...and this he would do by destroying everyone else."

As Mr. Ric wants Mr. Mignarda to "show his work", and as so far he has 
not, I will endeavor to
provide a few citations:

	In para 125 we used an analogy of a weak neighbor who is left 
destitute by a strong
	neighbor who takes all his land by forcing on him a series of 
compromises...The only 	
	sensible alternative for the weaker man is to kill the strong one 
while he has the chance.
	In the same way, while the industrial system is sick we must 
destroy it.  If we 	
            compromise with it and let it recover from its sickness, it 
will eventually wipe out all our 	
	freedom.  (para 135, Mad Genius edition p. 226)

This would, if taken literally, support the thesis.

But, in true TKian ambivalence, at para 140 we have

	The only way out is to dispense with the industrial-technological 
system altogether.
	This implies revolution, not necessarily an armed uprising, but 
certainly a
	radical and fundamental change in the nature of society.  (para 
140 p. 228)

And

	The factories should be destroyed, technical books burned, etc. 
(para 166, p. 238)

which Shadow has already cited.

Later on, though there is the lyrical passage in which FC says that

	freedom and dignity are more important than a long life or 
avoidance of physical
	pain.  Besides, we all have to die some time, and it may (note the 
"may", not "must")
	be better to die fighting for survival or for a cause, than to 
live a long but
	empty and purposeless life.  (para 168 p. 239)

One would think that someone whose motto is "Conformity is the Omnibus of 
Death" might
evince a tad of empathy for this, if not sympathy; in any event, this 
would seem to support that
FC wants to destroy himself, at least, with not the rest of the world 
still open to further debate.

Later again, however, the Manifesto writer says

	The kind of revolution we have in mind will not necessarily 
involve an armed
	uprising against any government.  It may or may not involve 
physical violence, but
	it will not be a POLITICAL revolution.  (para 193, p. 248).

Then, in complete opposition to Mr. Mignarda's thesis, and where I must 
confess I get off the
bandwagon, FC states:

	Revolutionaries should have as many children as they can.  There 
is strong
	scientific evidence (note that the antiscientist will drag in 
scientific support whenever it is
	to his benefit) that social attitudes are to a significant extent 
inherited...From our
	point of view it doesn't matter all that much whether the 
attitudes are passed on 	
            genetically or through childhood training.  In either case 
they ARE passed on.  (para
	204 p. 252)

and further

	...To ensure the strength of the next generation of 
revolutionaries the present generation
	should reproduce itself abundantly.  In doing so they will be 
worsening the population
	problem only slightly.  (para 205 p. 252)

It would appear that, contrary to Mr. Mignarda's opinion, FC, or TK, or 
whomever, wants to be
the CREATOR, not the destroyer!

However, helpfully FC also tells us that

	Throughout this article we've made imprecise statements and 
statements that
	ought to have all sorts of qualifications and reservations 
attached to them; and
	some of our statements may be flatly false.  (para 231 p. 261)

It looks like we have a draw here.  What are we left with here, besides 
"sound and fury,
signifying nothing?"  We are left with a portrait of an intelligent mind 
in such personal agony that
he might have indeed "gone beyond the framework of law", as Mr. Mignarda 
notes, in order to
communicate his ideas, because he could not communicate them otherwise on 
a more simple
human level.  This to me is the ultimate tragedy of the Kaczynski case, 
and has not much to do
with technology.  I suggest that whether we are dorks or geniuses, it is 
rare that we can truly
communicate with each other, and it is only through dumb luck, sheer human 
will, serendipitous
friendship, or the dreaded indoctrination/socialization that we are not in 
the same place as Ted
Kaczynski.  My personal prediction for 1997:  TK will languish in jail, 
and the point
counterpointing, citing, debating, flagellating, interpreting and positing 
will continue.

ellis windham
